# LockLens

**Open-source PostgreSQL monitoring and incident investigation.**

See what your databases are doing right now, find out who is blocking whom,
and keep the evidence when something goes wrong.

[CI](https://github.com/Huy-8bit/locklens/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[Backend image](https://hub.docker.com/r/johnnynguyen882/locklens-backend)
[Frontend image](https://hub.docker.com/r/johnnynguyen882/locklens-frontend)
PostgreSQL 14–18
[License: MIT](LICENSE)

[Quick start](#quick-start) · [Features](#features) · [Documentation](#documentation) · [Deployment](docs/deployment.md) · [Contributing](#contributing)

LockLens overview

## Why LockLens

- **One screen for the whole fleet.** Connections, query throughput and
  latency, replication, slow queries, sessions, blocking, and incidents for
  every instance of an environment.
- **Answers, not just charts.** Blocking chains with their root blocker,
  queries grouped by statement type, and findings that show the evidence,
  possible explanations, and what to check next.
- **Observe-only by design.** LockLens connects with a read-only role. It
  never cancels queries, terminates sessions, changes configuration, or runs
  DDL/DML on your databases.
- **Two small images.** A Go backend (API, collectors, CLI) and an nginx
  frontend that serves the web UI and proxies the API. Their only dependency
  is a PostgreSQL database for LockLens' own history.

## Features

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Monitor** | Fleet overview with environments (production, staging, …) · per-instance dashboards · sessions, transactions, cache, WAL, temp files, vacuum · replication topology with replay lag · host metrics from node_exporter |
| **Queries** | Every statement from `pg_stat_statements`, classified as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DDL, … · rate, time, and rows per type over time · top queries across instances · comparison with the previous period |
| **Investigate** | Blocking trees from `pg_blocking_pids()` with lock modes and wait times · idle-in-transaction blockers · 13 evidence-based rules · incident recorder with a timeline and stored blocking graphs |
| **Explore** *(opt-in)* | Browse schemas, tables, views, functions, types, indexes, and triggers · preview rows · read-only SQL editor with an execution-plan graph — never with an administrative role |
| **Team** | Users with roles: administrators manage everything, operators also preview rows and run read-only SQL, viewers only read · add an instance by pasting one connection string |
| **Operate** | Incident export to JSON and standalone HTML · Prometheus `/metrics` · health and readiness probes · retention · bounded buffering when the store is down |

     Queries by type
     Explorer
     SQL editor and plan

## Quick start

### Try the demo lab

Requires Docker with Compose v2 and `make`. It starts LockLens with a
PostgreSQL primary, two streaming standbys, and a background workload, all on
127.0.0.1 with fake, local-only credentials.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/Huy-8bit/locklens.git && cd locklens
make lab-up                      # first build takes a few minutes
```

Open   and sign in as `admin` / `locklens-lab-admin`.
Then create a problem and watch LockLens explain it:

```sh
make lab SCENARIO=chain          # an A → B → C blocking chain for 3 minutes
make lab-list                    # all scenarios
make lab-down                    # remove the lab and its data
```

See the [quickstart](docs/quickstart.md) for every scenario and what to expect.

### Run LockLens from the repository

Starts the backend, the frontend, and LockLens' own store; add your databases
in the UI.

```sh
make up                          # creates deploy/.env with random secrets and prints the admin password
make down                        # stop (data is kept)
```

### Run the Docker image

LockLens stores its history in its own PostgreSQL database (the *store*),
never in the databases it monitors.

```sh
export LOCKLENS_MASTER_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"   # keep it: it encrypts stored connection strings

docker network create locklens
docker run -d --name locklens-store --network locklens \
  -e POSTGRES_USER=locklens -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=change-me -e POSTGRES_DB=locklens \
  -v locklens-store:/var/lib/postgresql postgres:18-alpine

docker run -d --name locklens-backend --network locklens \
  -e LOCKLENS_STORE_DSN='postgres://locklens:change-me@locklens-store:5432/locklens?sslmode=disable' \
  -e LOCKLENS_MASTER_KEY \
  -e LOCKLENS_ADMIN_PASSWORD='choose-a-long-password' \
  -e LOCKLENS_COOKIE_SECURE=false \
  -e LOCKLENS_TRUSTED_PROXIES=locklens-frontend \
  johnnynguyen882/locklens-backend:latest

docker run -d --name locklens-frontend --network locklens -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \
  -e LOCKLENS_BACKEND_URL=http://locklens-backend:8080 \
  johnnynguyen882/locklens-frontend:latest
```

The frontend serves the UI and proxies `/api/` to the backend, so only the
frontend is published. Use the same released tag (`X.Y.Z`) for both images in
production, and put LockLens behind HTTPS before exposing it beyond your
machine (then drop `LOCKLENS_COOKIE_SECURE`). See [deployment](docs/deployment.md)
and [configuration](docs/configuration.md).

### Connect your databases

Monitored servers need PostgreSQL 14 or later and a login role with
`pg_read_all_stats` (no superuser). `pg_stat_statements` is optional but
recommended.

```sql
CREATE ROLE locklens_observer LOGIN PASSWORD '…';
GRANT pg_read_all_stats TO locklens_observer;
```

Then paste its connection string in **Settings → Add instance**. You can also
paste a superuser connection string: LockLens shows the statements it would run,
creates `locklens_monitor` and `locklens_reader` after you confirm, and stores
only those. Standbys reuse the roles of their primary.

### Build from source

Requires Go 1.26+ and Node.js 24.15+ (or 22.22.2+).

```sh
make build                       # web/dist (the UI) and bin/locklens (API server and CLI)
bin/locklens server              # needs LOCKLENS_STORE_DSN, LOCKLENS_MASTER_KEY, LOCKLENS_ADMIN_PASSWORD
make image                       # the two Docker images: locklens-backend:local, locklens-frontend:local
```

The backend serves only the API; serve the UI with the frontend image or, for
development, with `make dev` (Vite proxies `/api/` to a local backend).

## Command line

The CLI works directly against a database, without the server:

```sh
export LOCKLENS_DSN='postgres://observer@db.example.internal:5432/app?sslmode=verify-full'
locklens doctor                              # connectivity, version, privileges
locklens inspect                             # blocking chains and long transactions
locklens watch                               # live view, refreshed every 2 s
locklens snapshot save --out incident.json   # capture now, analyse offline later
```

```text
Blocking chains (blocker -> waiter)
  Incident 1: root blocker pid 116 blocks 1 directly, 2 in total
    pid 116  idle in transaction  tx 3s  user=demo_app  app=locklens-demo-A  blocks 1 directly, 2 in total
    └─ pid 117  active  lock wait 3s  tx 3s  user=demo_app  app=locklens-demo-B
       └─ pid 118  active  lock wait 3s  tx 3s  user=demo_app  app=locklens-demo-C
```

Reference: [CLI](docs/cli-reference.md).

## How it works

```text
                              backend (locklens server)                                frontend (nginx)
PostgreSQL targets ──read-only──► collectors ──► write queue ──► monitoring store
                                      │                                │
                                      ▼                                ▼
                           rules + incident recorder         REST API + live events ◄──/api/── web UI ◄── browser
```

One worker per target runs its collectors on a schedule under a global
concurrency limit. Counters become rates at ingest; restarts, statistics
resets, and gaps are stored as *unknown*, never as zero. More in
[architecture](docs/architecture.md) and [collectors](docs/collectors.md).

## Security and privacy

- Connection strings are encrypted at rest (AES-256-GCM) and never returned
  by the API or shown in the UI, logs, or exports.
- Users with roles (administrator, operator, viewer), bcrypt, server-side
  sessions, `HttpOnly` + `SameSite=Strict` cookies, and CSRF tokens. Listens on
  127.0.0.1 by default.
- SQL text is collected by default and can be switched off per instance.
- Row browsing and the SQL editor are off by default, limited to operators and
  administrators, never use an administrative role, and run inside read-only
  transactions. A superuser connection string is used once to create
  least-privilege roles and is never stored.

Details in [security](docs/security.md). To report a vulnerability, see
[SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).


### 账号与会话

- 支持密码登录与短信验证码登录，远端验证成功后才持久化账号。
- 自动处理登录过程中的滑块挑战；短信验证码保留人工输入环节。
- 密码、`token` 与 `satoken` 使用独立 AAD 的 AES-256-GCM 加密保存。
- 接口返回会话失效后自动标记账号，并提供按保存凭据重新登录的流程。
- 自动同步账号绑定的跑步计划、校园区域和服务端历史记录。

### 计划与规则

- 直接读取计划返回的距离、配速、步频、步幅、有效日期和允许运动时段。
- 支持按公里数或按次数计算的计划，并处理每日、每周次数与里程上限。
- 在规则有效范围的中间 70% 内动态抽样，避免长期使用固定参数。
- 任务执行前重新核对服务端记录与规则额度，超出限制时记录明确原因。

### 路线规划

- 基于地图步行路径服务构建围栏内路网，并随机选择路网节点规划路线。
- 道路数据不足时，自动切换为围栏内场地路线生成器。
- 支持服务端打卡点作为必经节点；起点、终点与路线形状均不强制闭环。
- 通过距离误差、重复率、越界率和打卡点覆盖率综合选择候选路线。
- 多 API Key 独立令牌桶、全局公平调度、重试、`singleflight` 请求合并。
- L1 进程内 LRU 与 L2 PostgreSQL 持久化缓存协同工作。

### 自动任务

- 支持固定时间与计划规定时段随机两种调度方式。
- 支持多 Worker × 多线程并发，配置可在控制台热更新。
- 计划、区域和距离均按账号资源自动约束。
- `next_run_at`、执行状态、远端记录号和失败原因全部持久化。
- 起跑前检查并异常结束遗留的阳光跑记录，复查确认后再开始；任一步失败时停止本次任务。
- 请求与采样按照客户端时间轴渐进执行，不集中突发发送。

### 数据与可观测性

- 运行记录包含距离、配速、步数、步频、步幅、分段与地图轨迹。
- 内置一致性预检，展示状态解释与无效原因，而不是原始响应堆栈。
- 地图指标包含各 Key QPS、令牌发放、缓存命中、重试、排队和在途请求。
- 提供健康检查、运行配置、OpenAPI 描述和结构化请求日志。

## 🗺 系统架构

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    UI[React 控制台] --> API[Go HTTP API]
    API --> ACC[账号与会话]
    API --> JOB[任务调度器]
    API --> ROUTE[路线规划器]
    ACC --> PROTO[协议适配层]
    JOB --> RUNNER[运行编排器]
    RUNNER --> ROUTE
    RUNNER --> PROTO
    ROUTE --> GATE[多 Key 公平令牌桶]
    GATE --> MAP[地图路径服务]
    ACC --> DB[(PostgreSQL)]
    JOB --> DB
    ROUTE --> CACHE[L1 LRU / L2 PostgreSQL]
    CACHE --> DB
```

一次自动任务的主要流程：

```text
读取账号会话 → 校验计划与额度 → 获取起跑上下文/打卡点
→ 生成候选路线 → 按真实时间轴生成与发送数据
→ 完成结算 → 保存执行结果与远端记录号
```

## 📦 快速开始

### 选择部署方式

| 方式 | 适用场景 | 入口 |
|---|---|---|
| Docker Compose | 新部署，同时启动应用和数据库 | 下方快速开始 |
| 完整发行包 | 已有 PostgreSQL，不想安装 Go / Node.js | [下载最新版本](https://github.com/Zolohacker/EasyRun/releases/latest) |
| Windows 本地源码 | 本地开发与调试 | 下方本地运行说明 |

发行包提供 Windows amd64、Linux amd64 / arm64，包含前端、模型和对应平台运行库，附 `checksums.txt`。解压后配置数据库连接，从解压目录启动；启用在线更新还需独立守护进程，见 [启动与更新说明](./docs/updates.md#启动方式)。Linux 使用 glibc 环境并准备 `libstdc++6`、`libgomp1`；arm64 本地推理尚待真实硬件验收。

### Docker Compose

准备环境：Docker Engine 24+、Docker Compose v2。

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Zolohacker/EasyRun.git
cd EasyRun
cp .env.example .env
```

编辑 `.env` 配置随机数据库密码（建议字母数字）：

```dotenv
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=USE_A_RANDOM_ALPHANUMERIC_PASSWORD
COOKIE_SECURE=false
```

首次启动自动生成并保存主密钥到 `data/account-master.key`（Docker 使用持久卷）。无需手填主密钥和地图 Key；初始化后按总览提示，在「系统配置 → 地图与执行器」添加地图 Web 服务 Key。人脸模型与三平台推理库随包提供，启动自动识别路径。[首次启动、备份与旧部署迁移](./docs/first-run.md)。

首次访问直接设置超级管理员邮箱、密码及使用模式，无需额外令牌；本机、容器和反向代理部署使用相同流程。正式 HTTPS 部署把 `COOKIE_SECURE` 设置为 `true`。

启动：

```bash
docker compose up -d --build
```

访问：[本地控制台](http://127.0.0.1:8080/)。

首次设置顺序：**设置超管 → 选择使用模式 → 在系统配置添加地图 Key → 添加账号**。初始化后请备份数据库、`data/account-master.key` 与钱包助记词；不要删除持久卷进行升级。

### Windows 本地源码运行

准备环境：Go 1.23+、PostgreSQL 17 客户端工具；启用本地人脸推理需可用的 GCC / CGO 工具链。仓库已包含构建后的前端，仅修改前端时需要 Node.js 20+。

```powershell

Set-Location EasyRun
```

## 🧭 基本使用

| 运行总览 | 查看账号就绪情况、排期、执行状态、服务健康与版本更新 |
| 账号矩阵 | 添加账号、维护会话、查看计划进度与历史详情；管理人脸设置与修改链接 |

# Rove: the agent multiplexer for your terminal

Rove is a terminal-native workspace for running multiple coding tasks in parallel with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code), [Codex](https://github.com/openai/codex), [Copilot](https://github.com/github/copilot-cli), Kimi, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Cursor Agent, [and more](./docs/ENGINES.md), or any CLI you register.

Rove isolates parallel work in git worktrees and branches, while agent and shell sessions keep running when you disconnect.

    Documentation   ·
   Quick start  ·
   Concepts  ·
   CLI  ·
   Agent API  ·
   Website

The sidebar tracks tasks and their sessions. The workspace embeds the active agent or shell. The files pane shows what changed in the worktree. Switch tasks to read output, inspect a diff, run tests, or send the next instruction.

## Quick start

Install Rove, then launch it in a repository. Rove runs on [Bun](https://bun.sh) ≥ 1.3.11, and the install script sets Bun up if you don't have it.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://rove.run/install.sh | sh
cd your-repo
rove
```

Press `n` to create your first task. You need git and at least one supported agent CLI on `PATH`; other install methods are under [Install](#install).

To let a coding agent drive Rove itself, install the skill:

```bash
rove skill install
```

## What you get

- **Parallel tasks, isolated in git.** Each task owns a worktree and branch, so a refactor, a bug fix, and a review move at the same time without agents overwriting each other's files.
- **Every agent CLI, side by side.** Each task picks its engine: Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Kimi, Pi, OMP, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Cursor Agent, [and more](./docs/ENGINES.md), or a CLI you register. Rove runs the real CLI, with its own auth, permissions, and models.
- **Sessions that outlive the terminal.** Quit the TUI or drop SSH, then reattach later. The agents keep working on the host.
- **Terminal-native.** No desktop app. Run Rove where the code lives: laptop, devbox, VPS, or a narrow mobile SSH session.
- **Scriptable.** Scripts and coding agents create, inspect, message, and land tasks through `rove api`.

## How it works

```text
Managed task
├── git worktree
├── git branch
└── terminal tabs
    ├── Claude Code
    ├── Codex
    └── shell
```

Tabs inside one task share its files, so work that needs isolation gets its own managed task; project-main tasks and `rove .` directory tasks deliberately reuse an existing directory. Sessions run on the host rather than in your terminal window, so they keep going when the TUI detaches and come back when you run `rove` again. The loop: start several tasks, switch between their live sessions, review each worktree's diff and checks, send follow-up instructions, then merge the branches that worked out. [Concepts](./docs/CONCEPTS.md) and [Sessions](./docs/SESSIONS.md) cover the full lifecycle.

## Install

The install script above sets up the Bun runtime Rove needs, then Rove itself. Or use the package manager you already have:

```bash
npm install -g @sma1lboy/rove   # offers to install Bun on first launch
bun install -g @sma1lboy/rove   # if you already run Bun
npx @sma1lboy/rove              # try it without installing
```

Rove runs on macOS, Linux, and Windows; Windows also requires Node.js and Git for Windows/Git Bash. The CLI runs on [Bun](https://bun.sh) ≥ 1.3.11, which every install route brings along. If your Bun lives somewhere unusual, point Rove at it with `ROVE_BUN=/path/to/bun`.

`rove` is the canonical command. The package also installs `rove` as a compatibility alias. On first launch, supported legacy state is copied into `~/.rove`; existing files and worktrees stay where they are.

## Scripting and Agent API

`rove api` exposes the same task model to shell scripts and coding agents. A run creates a task, checks its output, sends follow-ups, and lands the branch:

```bash
rove api add --repo "$PWD" --prompt "Fix the flaky auth test."
rove api list
rove api read-output --task-id
rove api send --task-id   --prompt "Run the integration suite too."
rove api land --task-id
```

The companion skill teaches a coding agent to drive that loop for you:

```bash
rove skill install
```

A task created from inside another Rove session remembers which task and tab dispatched it, so workers report results back without an external coordinator. The API also covers task inspection, notifications, prompts, panes, issue tracking, routines, and worktree-safe lifecycle operations.

Every verb, flag, and exit code is in the [Agent API reference](https://docs.rove.run/rove/api).

## Plugins

A plugin is a directory with a `rove-plugin.toml` manifest and commands in any language. It can add panes, react to events such as a finished agent turn, register commands and settings, and contribute whole engines. Browse and install from the terminal:

```bash
rove plugin search
rove plugin install owner/repo
```

The same catalog is on [rove.run/plugins](https://rove.run/plugins) and under Settings → Marketplace. Any public GitHub repo tagged `rove-plugin` shows up there; [plugin authoring](./docs/PLUGIN-AUTHORING.md) covers the manifest, the event catalog, and the optional TypeScript SDK.

A plugin can also ship a **mod**: one long-running process that draws panes of text, buttons, and input fields. The TUI and the browser client (`rove --web`) draw the same pane from the same data, so a button pressed in either one updates both. Mods appear on the rail's Mods page; see [Mods](./docs/PLUGIN-AUTHORING.md#mods) and the [`counter-mod` example](./packages/rove-plugin-sdk/examples/counter-mod).

## More features

- **Review.** Diff views, plus inline notes that go back as one agent prompt.
- **Recovery.** Rate-limit resume, cross-engine handoff, several agents inside one task.
- **Remote ergonomics.** Narrow and mobile layouts, a durable Inbox, notifications, attachments.
- **Unattended work.** Scheduled routines, with optional prechecks that skip idle runs.
- **Planning context.** Local Kanban, GitHub issue intake, reusable repository field notes.
- **Customization.** Themes, and [plugins](#plugins) with custom panes, events, commands, engines, and mods.

Details live in the [TUI guide](./docs/TUI.md), [Routines](./docs/ROUTINES.md), [configuration](./docs/CONFIGURATION.md), and [plugin authoring](./docs/PLUGIN-AUTHORING.md).

## Troubleshooting

```bash
rove doctor
```

[Troubleshooting](./docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md) has the diagnostics and recovery steps.

## Development

```bash
bun install
bun run dev:sandbox
bun run test
```

Start with [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Architecture](./docs/ARCHITECTURE.md). Shipped behavior is in the [changelog](./packages/rove/CHANGELOG.md).

**EventPilot AI** is an autonomous, production-ready enterprise event planning SaaS platform. It eliminates event coordination friction by synthesizing multi-day schedules, vendor procurement breakdowns, budget allocations, run sheets, and catering specifications in seconds.

Operating on a **100% private local AI inference architecture**, EventPilot AI utilizes Google's **Gemma 2B** running via **Ollama**. No third-party cloud API keys, tokens, or external subscriptions are required. # MyDB

**A high-performance database, compatible with MySQL**

Let agents manage data flexibly — transactions, analytics, and vector search in a single database.

[Download](https://github.com/yzsind/mydb/releases/tag/v1.0.0) · [Performance evaluation](#performance-evaluation) · [Quick Start](#quick-start) · [Built for AI Agents](#built-for-ai-agents) · [Documentation](docs/README.md) · [MySQL Compatibility](docs/mysql80-compatibility.md)

---

MyDB is a general-purpose database built in Rust, designed around three directions: **AI agents, high-performance hybrid transactional/analytical processing (HTAP), and MySQL compatibility**. Through a familiar SQL interface, applications and agents can manage business data, evolve table schemas, run real-time analytics, and search similar vectors — without copying data across systems or maintaining multiple interfaces.

MyDB 1.0.0 is a public-preview release intended for feature validation and controlled-environment evaluation. It is not yet a production-grade MySQL replacement, and on-disk formats are not guaranteed to be backward compatible.

| Core capability | What it gives you |
| --- | --- |
| **Built for AI agents** | Online schema changes, automatic zone maps, and native vector data management reduce manual work in schema evolution and query tuning. |
| **High-performance HTAP** | Parallel hash joins, vectorized execution, and a cost-based optimizer power both transactional and analytical workloads. |
| **MySQL compatible** | Reuse MySQL clients, JDBC drivers, core SQL, and row binlog integration. |

## Performance evaluation

**MyDB vs. MySQL 8.0** :

| Workload | MyDB | MySQL | Advantage |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Point queries · 100M rows, 20 clients | 316,968 queries/s | 174,566 queries/s | **1.82x throughput** |
| Read-only transactions · 100M rows, 20 clients | 14,323 transactions/s | 7,294 transactions/s | **1.96x throughput** |
| TPC-H-derived analytics · SF=10, 22 query medians summed | 57.727 s | 882.784 s | **15.29x speedup** |
| TPC-DS-derived analytics · SF=10, 55 matching query files | 113.968 s | 2,576.552 s | **22.61x speedup** |
| Bulk import · TPC-H SF=10, `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE` | 25.708 s | 357.495 s | **13.91x speedup** |

Same 16-vCPU host, 10 GiB database memory limits, and durable commits; results
cover different development builds and TPC-derived results are unaudited. See
the [detailed comparison](docs/performance-comparison.md) for all results, test
conditions, and limitations.

## Quick Start

Download prebuilt packages for macOS ARM64, Linux x86_64, and Windows x64 from the
[1.0.0 release page](https://github.com/yzsind/mydb/releases/tag/v1.0.0), which also
includes SHA256 checksums and platform validation details.

### Run a downloaded binary

Download the package for your platform, extract it, and open a terminal in the
directory containing the executable. On macOS or Linux, start it with:

```bash
chmod +x ./mydb
./mydb --data-dir ./data
```

On Windows, run the equivalent command in PowerShell:

```powershell
.\mydb.exe --data-dir ./data
```

The server listens locally on port `8738` and stores data in `./data`. No Rust
toolchain or config file is needed. With a MySQL 8.0 client installed, connect
from another terminal:

```bash
mysql -h127.0.0.1 -P8738 -uroot -proot  test
```

A fresh data directory includes the `test` database and the local `root` account
with password `root`. Run `SELECT 1;` to check the connection. Enter `quit` to
exit the client, then press **Ctrl+C** in the server terminal to stop it. Restart
with the same data directory to reopen your data.

### Build and connect

Install Rust 1.95 or newer, a native C toolchain, Perl, and a MySQL 8.0 client;
the shell commands below target macOS and Linux.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/yzsind/mydb.git
cd mydb
cargo build --release --locked --bin mydb

MYDB_DATA_DIR=/tmp/mydb/data \
  ./target/release/mydb --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8738
```

When the server is ready, connect from another terminal:

```bash
mysql -h127.0.0.1 -P8738 -uroot -proot --ssl-mode=REQUIRED test
```

A fresh data directory creates `root@localhost` with password `root` and a `test`
database. This account accepts only loopback connections. `MYDB_ROOT_PASSWORD`
sets the initial password on first start; it does not change existing accounts.
The default protocol port is `8738`; override it with `--port`.

Try a write, an aggregate, and a window function:

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    region VARCHAR(32),
    amount DECIMAL(12, 2)
);

INSERT INTO orders VALUES
    (1, 'east', 120.00),
    (2, 'south', 80.00),
    (3, 'east', 180.00);

SELECT region,
       SUM(amount) AS revenue,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(amount) DESC) AS revenue_rank
FROM orders
GROUP BY region
ORDER BY revenue_rank, region;
```

Exit with `quit`, then stop the server with **Ctrl+C**. Restarting with the same
data directory reopens the data, so the CREATE and INSERT statements only need to
run once; `/tmp/mydb/data` is temporary storage and may be removed by the OS.

### Persistent data and configuration

For a separate, persistent instance, write a config file (data directory,
durability mode, `memory_target`) and start with `--config`; the server reads a
config file only when `--config` is supplied, and the Docker entrypoint supplies
its default config automatically. `strict` (the default durability mode)
synchronizes WAL before acknowledging a commit, and `memory_target` is a
working-set target — not a hard process memory limit — defaulting to 50% of
detected effective memory. See [configuration](docs/configuration.md) and
[hardware and OS requirements](docs/hardware-and-os-requirements.md) for all
settings, durability modes, and sizing.

### Application connections and TLS

TLS is advertised by default with an ephemeral self-signed certificate when none
is configured; for remote deployments, configure a trusted certificate and verify
the server identity (see [TLS configuration](docs/configuration.md#tls)).
Runnable [Java, Python, Go, C++, and Rust examples](examples/README.md) cover
connections, typed queries, DDL/DML, batches, transactions, and stored procedure
calls, including JDBC URLs for local evaluation.

### Docker

Build and run a container (stop any local instance using port `8738` first):

```bash
docker build -t mydb:local .
docker volume create mydb-data

docker run --name mydb \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8738:8738 \
  -v mydb-data:/var/lib/mydb \
  -e MYDB_ROOT_PASSWORD='change-me' \
  mydb:local

docker exec -it mydb mysql -h127.0.0.1 -P8738 -uroot -p --ssl
```

Enter `change-me` for the password on a fresh volume. Stop with `docker stop
mydb` and restart with `docker start mydb`; the named volume retains the data.
Bridge/NAT connections through the published port do not match `root@localhost` —
create a dedicated account in that SQL session for host connections. Local image
builds enable TLS, `fast-alloc`, and the MySQL replication receiver by default.
See the [Docker deployment guide](docs/docker.md) for certificates, mounted
configuration, cross-architecture builds, and connecting from the host.

### Platforms and distribution

Supported operating systems: macOS (arm64 and Intel) and Linux (x86_64 and
aarch64), plus Windows 11 for foreground operation on local NTFS. See
[hardware and OS requirements](docs/hardware-and-os-requirements.md) for
verification details, Windows limitations, and distribution scope.

## Architecture

MyDB architecture: protocol, SQL engine, unified memory management, storage engine, transactions, backup and recovery, primary-replica HA, sessions, security, and metadata; highlighting the optimizer, executor, heap tables, Zone Map, HNSW, online DDL, unified memory management, and directly queryable backups

## Built for AI Agents

An agent's data needs change with every task: add a column, build an index, write embeddings, then join retrieval results back to business data. MyDB keeps all of this inside one transactional database.

### Smart indexing: fewer full scans without manual indexes

MyDB enables automatic **zone maps** on persistent user tables by default: per-block statistics let queries skip data blocks that cannot match a predicate, often turning a full scan into a small range read on tables with no hand-built B-tree index. Pruning is conservative — whenever statistics are missing or a predicate cannot be proven safe, the executor falls back to a regular scan. See the [feature overview](docs/feature-overview.md) for how the mechanism and fallbacks work.

### Online DDL: schemas that evolve with the task

MyDB minimizes DDL locking and query waiting by coordinating schema versions, index builds, and concurrent access in the native storage layer:

- **Online index and primary key creation**: regular and unique B-tree indexes and newly added primary keys allow concurrent DML while being built.
- **Read-compatible column changes**: adding columns without storage rewrites, compatible type modifications, and some metadata-only changes keep ordinary queries running.
- **Constraints and charset settings**: online foreign keys, CHECK constraints, and default charset/collation metadata changes.

"Lock-free DDL" is a design direction, not a current guarantee: publication still coordinates with write transactions, and replacing primary keys, rewriting column data, or converting charsets still takes locks. See [ALTER TABLE](docs/statements/ddl/alter-table.md) and the [DDL compatibility boundaries](docs/mysql80-compatibility.md#table-ddl).

### Native vectors: from storage to large-scale similarity search

- **Native `VECTOR(n, datatype)` type**: FLOAT32 (default), FLOAT16, BFLOAT16, INT8, and BINARY retain their native payloads. Numeric vectors support L2, cosine, and dot-product distance; BINARY supports Hamming and Jaccard. Dimension limits depend on the datatype, from 16,383 for FLOAT32 to 524,256 bits for BINARY.
- **HNSW and IVF indexes**: both support memory and paged storage. Paged index pages participate in the buffer pool and WAL, allowing index payloads to exceed memory capacity; exact KNN scans are also available.
- **Explicit quantization**: `WITH (quantization=sq8|sq4|pq|bq)` compresses numeric index payloads, with final re-ranking against visible heap values. The default is `none`; search breadth and re-ranking budgets determine the recall, memory, and latency tradeoff.
- **Unified SQL**: the optimizer recognizes `ORDER BY distance LIMIT k` and supports parameterized queries; vector writes participate in transaction commit and rollback.

Combined with JSONB, full-text, and structured queries, this supports semantic search, knowledge retrieval, and agent memory. See [vector datatypes and indexes](docs/vector-indexes.md) for options, training, limits, and recovery, and the [vector function reference](docs/function/vector/README.md). The current implementation is HNSW / IVF; disk residency does not imply a complete DiskANN implementation.

### Try vector retrieval and RETURNING

Still in the `test` database, create a small collection on a `VECTOR` column
declared `NOT NULL`; `RETURNING` gives the inserted IDs directly to the caller:

```sql
CREATE TABLE agent_notes (
    id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    content VARCHAR(128),
    embedding VECTOR(3) NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO agent_notes VALUES
    (1, 'order summary', STRING_TO_VECTOR('[1,0,0]')),
    (2, 'shipping details', STRING_TO_VECTOR('[1,1,0]')),
    (3, 'account settings', STRING_TO_VECTOR('[0,0,2]'))
RETURNING id;

CREATE INDEX idx_agent_notes_embedding ON agent_notes (embedding)
USING HNSW WITH (metric=l2);

SELECT id, content,
       L2_DISTANCE(embedding, STRING_TO_VECTOR('[1,0,0]')) AS distance
FROM agent_notes
ORDER BY distance
LIMIT 2;
```

The INSERT returns IDs `1`, `2`, `3`; the query returns the two rows nearest to
`[1,0,0]` by L2 distance. HNSW provides approximate nearest-neighbor search —
recall and performance on larger collections d

## See Flovart in action

Two 60-second promo cuts — v2 (8 MB) and v4 (27 MB, higher bitrate):

         Promo cut v2.  60 seconds ·  source file

         Promo cut v4.  60 seconds ·  source file

    The current recorded Agent/Workflow surface — natural language becomes nodes and edges.

    Flovart Vision · 3 minutes.  Click the image to watch the film.

This film is the **north star for Flovart product interaction and UI**. The product we are building should feel like this:

- **Stay in the editor first.** Resolve remains the source of truth; Flovart appears as a narrow contextual layer around the clip you are already working on.
- **Draw where. Say what. Get a layer.** Point at the frame, describe the intent, then generate reviewable AI-layer candidates instead of replacing the source clip.
- **Candidates before commits.** Compare results visually, keep every version, and never let a late result silently replace the version you explicitly chose.
- **Human + Agent, one visible state.** Agent activity, revisions and out-of-date results are visible on the same Workflow that the creator can edit by hand.
- **Open the full Flovart canvas only when the job needs it.** Multi-step references, stale branches, version history and more complex production expand into the visual Workflow instead of turning the host panel into a second app.
- **Return to the host non-destructively.** Approved results flow back through a reviewable handoff — Media Pool first, then a new layer/track only when that host capability is actually verified.
- **Local-first by default.** Footage, project context and durable results stay close to the creator's machine; external model calls are explicit and provider-scoped.

## Quick start

### For creators

1. Download a preview build from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/avabbbb/Flovart/releases).

Run from a source checkout while the versioned CLI package remains a release gate:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/avabbbb/Flovart.git
cd Flovart
npm install
npm run flovart:cli -- start --source --web --open

```

Then ask your local agent: **“Open Flovart and work on this Workflow.”**

Your agent learns Flovart through the **Agent Integration Skill** at `.agents/skills/flovart/` (mirrored for Claude under `.claude/skills/flovart/` and bundled for WorkBuddy under `integrations/workbuddy/flovart/skills/flovart/`). This is a thin adapter — it teaches the agent the 5 operations below; it is not a Production Skill / Marketplace feature.

The normal agent loop is `status`, `workflow.inspect`, `workflow.selection.get`, `workflow.apply` and `workflow.node.run`. Connection setup and diagnostics use `ensure` and `doctor`; development-only browser checks are covered in the [Getting Started guide](docs/overview/quick-start.en.md).

## Feature tour

Every clip below is a real recording of the running app — one operation, start to finish, with no composited frames and no mockups. Each is cut to the action.

**Agent-native, not screen-scraping.** These are operations on the same Workflow an agent drives. The hero above and the CLI capture under [Architecture](#architecture) are agent-driven end to end, with no human input; the tour below is that same surface driven by hand, because that is the path a new user follows first. Node creation, connections, selection, viewport, node moves and resizes, and the node tools are all exposed to agents as typed operations — with revision and idempotency boundaries rather than coordinates on a screen.

Video and audio tools run ffmpeg.wasm in the browser; their core is pre-warmed before the recorded action, so the clip shows the operation rather than the one-off ~30MB wasm download — **clip length is therefore not the wait time on a first run**. ### Canvas

         Arrange by hand.  Nodes move freely; the graph itself is the state.

         Tidy.  One click re-lays out the whole graph.

         Prompt in place.  Select a node and write the prompt on the node itself — no separate prompt dialog.

### Image nodes

Four local operations on the same generated fixture plate, each producing a real result node. None of them contacts a model service.

         Crop.  Set the crop rectangle, then apply.

         Rotate and flip.  Quarter turns and mirrors.

         Split to grid.  Each cell becomes its own connected image node.

         Grade.  Colour adjustments preview live before they are applied.

### Video nodes

Also local, also without a model service: these run through the in-browser ffmpeg core, and each one creates its own result node (audio/video split creates two).

         Trim.  Set the in/out points; the cut uses stream copy, so nothing is re-encoded.

         Split audio and video.  One video becomes a silent video node plus an audio node.

         Merge.  Select several video nodes and join them in order.

         Extract a frame.  Pick a timecode and get an image node out of the video.

         First frame.  One click, straight to an image node.

         Last frame.  Same, from the tail of the clip.

### Audio nodes

         Trim.  Same in/out controls, same stream-copy cut.

         Speed.  0.25×–4× with pitch preserved.

         Separate vocals and backing.  Two audio nodes come out; this is stereo phase cancellation, so mono or heavily mixed material separates less cleanly.

### The external-agent link

         Operations land on the canvas.  Driven entirely by the agent — no human input —  workflow.node.create  and  workflow.connect  run through the typed CLI while the visible Workflow updates in place: no screen scraping, no hidden copy of the project.

         Open the Agent surface.  Reachable from the same canvas toolbar.

Not filmed yet, and deliberately not shown: model-backed generation and the model-backed image tools (image generation, upscale, background removal, layer split, edit/outpaint) — this checkout configures no provider, so there is no honest result to record. That gap is logged in the [recording notes](docs/archive/2026-10-07/maintenance/readme/DEMO_RECORDING.md).

## Why Flovart?

Most AI creative tools ask you to move your work into another canvas. **Flovart goes the other way.**

Your professional editor remains the source of truth. Your Agent reads the creative context. Flovart manages generation, references, durable artifacts and reviewable candidates — and the full Flovart workspace opens only when the job actually needs a visual Workflow.

- **Inside the editor.** The first host path targets DaVinci Resolve Studio 21.1; other creative hosts remain Experimental until real-host validation.
- **Agent-native.** Agents act through typed Flovart capabilities and host-native control surfaces instead of mouse coordinates or screen scraping.
- **Non-destructive by default.** Generated work starts as a candidate. The Resolve-first P0 ends at **Add to Media Pool** before timeline replacement is considered.
- **Bring your own models.** Keep the providers, models and API keys you choose.
- **Local-first.** Project-adjacent state, references and generated artifacts stay close to the creative workspace wherever the current implementation supports it.

The canvas is still a power surface for multi-shot work, complex references and reusable workflows. **It is no longer the product premise.**

## Core capabilities

| Capability | Flovart |
| --- | --- |
| Agent control | Typed operations against the actual visible Workflow |
| Human editing | The same graph, assets and results stay directly editable |

repositories.description: Distributed SQL database in Rust - Raft, MVCC, SQL engine.
repositories.readmeExcerpt:
#    toyDB

Distributed SQL database in Rust, built from scratch as an educational project. Main features:

* [Raft distributed consensus][raft] for linearizable state machine replication.

* [ACID transactions][txn] with MVCC-based snapshot isolation.

* [Pluggable storage engine][storage] with [BitCask][bitcask] and [in-memory][memory] backends.

* [Iterator-based query engine][query] with [heuristic optimization][optimizer] and time-travel
  support.

* [SQL interface][sql] including joins, aggregates, and transactions.

toyDB is intended to be simple and understandable, and also functional and correct. Other aspects
like performance, scalability, and availability are non-goals -- these are major sources of
complexity in production-grade databases, and obscure the basic underlying concepts. Shortcuts have
been taken where possible.

I originally wrote toyDB in 2020 to learn more about database internals. Since then, I've spent
several years building real distributed SQL databases at
[CockroachDB](https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach) and
[Neon](https://github.com/neondatabase/neon). Based on this experience, I've rewritten toyDB as a
simple illustration of the architecture and concepts behind distributed SQL databases.

[raft]: https://github.com/erikgrinaker/toydb/blob/main/src/raft/mod.rs
[txn]: https://github.com/erikgrinaker/toydb/blob/main/src/storage/mvcc.rs
[storage]: https://github.com/erikgrinaker/toydb/blob/main/src/storage/engine.rs
[bitcask]: https://github.com/erikgrinaker/toydb/blob/main/src/storage/bitcask.rs
[memory]: https://github.com/erikgrinaker/toydb/blob/main/src/storage/memory.rs
[query]: https://github.com/erikgrinaker/toydb/blob/main/src/sql/execution/executor.rs
[optimizer]: https://github.com/erikgrinaker/toydb/blob/main/src/sql/planner/optimizer.rs
[sql]: https://github.com/erikgrinaker/toydb/blob/main/src/sql/parser/parser.rs

## Documentation

* [Architecture guide](docs/architecture/index.md): a guided tour of toyDB's code and architecture.

* [SQL examples](docs/examples.md): walkthrough of toyDB's SQL features.

* [SQL reference](docs/sql.md): reference documentation for toyDB's SQL dialect.

* [References](docs/references.md): research materials used while building toyDB.

## Usage

With a [Rust compiler](https://www.rust-lang.org/tools/install) installed, a local five-node
cluster can be built and started as:

```
$ ./cluster/run.sh
Starting 5 nodes on ports 9601-9605 with data under cluster/*/data/.
To connect to node 1, run: cargo run --release --bin toysql

toydb4 21:03:55 [INFO] Listening on [::1]:9604 (SQL) and [::1]:9704 (Raft)
toydb1 21:03:55 [INFO] Listening on [::1]:9601 (SQL) and [::1]:9701 (Raft)
toydb2 21:03:55 [INFO] Listening on [::1]:9602 (SQL) and [::1]:9702 (Raft)
toydb3 21:03:55 [INFO] Listening on [::1]:9603 (SQL) and [::1]:9703 (Raft)
toydb5 21:03:55 [INFO] Listening on [::1]:9605 (SQL) and [::1]:9705 (Raft)
toydb2 21:03:56 [INFO] Starting new election for term 1
[...]
toydb2 21:03:56 [INFO] Won election for term 1, becoming leader
```

A command-line client can be built and used with node 1 on `localhost:9601`:

```
$ cargo run --release --bin toysql
Connected to toyDB node n1. Enter !help for instructions.
toydb> CREATE TABLE movies (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR NOT NULL);
toydb> INSERT INTO movies VALUES (1, 'Sicario'), (2, 'Stalker'), (3, 'Her');
toydb> SELECT * FROM movies;
1, 'Sicario'
2, 'Stalker'
3, 'Her'
```

toyDB supports most common SQL features, including joins, aggregates, and transactions. Below is an
`EXPLAIN` query plan of a more complex query (fetches all movies from studios that have released any
movie with an IMDb rating of 8 or more):

```
toydb> EXPLAIN SELECT m.title, g.name AS genre, s.name AS studio, m.rating
  FROM movies m JOIN genres g ON m.genre_id = g.id,
    studios s JOIN movies good ON good.studio_id = s.id AND good.rating >= 8
  WHERE m.studio_id = s.id
  GROUP BY m.title, g.name, s.name, m.rating, m.released
  ORDER BY m.rating DESC, m.released ASC, m.title ASC;

Remap: m.title, genre, studio, m.rating (dropped: m.released)
└─ Order: m.rating desc, m.released asc, m.title asc
   └─ Projection: m.title, g.name as genre, s.name as studio, m.rating, m.released
      └─ Aggregate: m.title, g.name, s.name, m.rating, m.released
         └─ HashJoin: inner on m.studio_id = s.id
            ├─ HashJoin: inner on m.genre_id = g.id
            │  ├─ Scan: movies as m
            │  └─ Scan: genres as g
            └─ HashJoin: inner on s.id = good.studio_id
               ├─ Scan: studios as s
               └─ Scan: movies as good (good.rating > 8 OR good.rating = 8)
```

## Architecture

toyDB's architecture is fairly typical for a distributed SQL database: a transactional
key/value store managed by a Raft cluster with a SQL query engine on top. See the
[architecture guide](./docs/architecture/index.md) for more details.

[toyDB architecture](./docs/architecture/index.md)

## Tests

toyDB mainly uses [Goldenscripts](https://github.com/erikgrinaker/goldenscript) for tests. These
script various scenarios, capture events and output, and later assert that the behavior remains the
same. See e.g.:

* [Raft cluster tests](https://github.com/erikgrinaker/toydb/tree/main/src/raft/testscripts/node)
* [MVCC transaction tests](https://github.com/erikgrinaker/toydb/tree/main/src/storage/testscripts/mvcc)
* [SQL execution tests](https://github.com/erikgrinaker/toydb/tree/main/src/sql/testscripts)
* [End-to-end tests](https://github.com/erikgrinaker/toydb/tree/main/tests/scripts)

Run tests with `cargo test`, or have a look at the latest
[CI run](https://github.com/erikgrinaker/toydb/actions/workflows/ci.yml).

## Benchmarks

toyDB is not optimized for performance, but comes with a `workload` benchmark tool that can run
various workloads against a toyDB cluster. For example:

```sh
# Start a 5-node toyDB cluster.
$ ./cluster/run.sh
[...]

# Run a read-only benchmark via all 5 nodes.
$ cargo run --release --bin workload read
Preparing initial dataset... done (0.179s)
Spawning 16 workers... done (0.006s)
Running workload read (rows=1000 size=64 batch=1)...

Time   Progress     Txns      Rate       p50       p90       p99      pMax
1.0s      13.1%    13085   13020/s     1.3ms     1.5ms     1.9ms     8.4ms
2.0s      27.2%    27183   13524/s     1.3ms     1.5ms     1.8ms     8.4ms
3.0s      41.3%    41301   13702/s     1.2ms     1.5ms     1.8ms     8.4ms
4.0s      55.3%    55340   13769/s     1.2ms     1.5ms     1.8ms     8.4ms
5.0s      70.0%    70015   13936/s     1.2ms     1.5ms     1.8ms     8.4ms
6.0s      84.7%    84663   14047/s     1.2ms     1.4ms     1.8ms     8.4ms
7.0s      99.6%    99571   14166/s     1.2ms     1.4ms     1.7ms     8.4ms
7.1s     100.0%   100000   14163/s     1.2ms     1.4ms     1.7ms     8.4ms

Verifying dataset... done (0.002s)
```

The available workloads are:

* `read`: single-row primary key lookups.
* `write`: single-row inserts to sequential primary keys.
* `bank`: bank transfers between various customers and accounts. To make things interesting, this
  includes joins, secondary indexes, sorting, and conflicts.

For more information about workloads and parameters, run `cargo run --bin workload -- --help`.

Example workload results are listed below. Write performance is atrocious, due to
[fsync](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sync_(Unix)) and a lack of write batching in the Raft layer.
Disabling fsync, or using the in-memory engine, significantly improves write performance (at the
expense of durability).

| Workload | BitCask     | BitCask w/o fsync | Memory      |
|----------|-------------|-------------------|-------------|
| `read`   | 14163 txn/s | 13941 txn/s       | 13949 txn/s |
| `write`  | 35 txn/s    | 4719 txn/s        | 7781 txn/s  |
| `bank`   | 21 txn/s    | 1120 txn/s        | 1346 txn/s  |

## Debugging

[VSCode](https://code.visualstudio.com) and the [CodeLLDB](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=vadimcn.vscode-lldb)
extension can be used to debug toyDB, with the debug configuration under `.vscode/launch.json`.

Under the "Run and Debug" tab, select e.g. "Debug executable 'toydb'" or "Debug unit tests in
library 'toydb'".

## Documentation

## Quick Start

### 1️⃣ Install Docker & Docker Compose

Ensure you have [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) and [Docker Compose](https://docs.docker.com/compose/install/) installed.

### 2️⃣ Create docker-compose.yml

Create a `docker-compose.yml` file with content:

```yaml
services:
  # PostgreSQL Database Service
  postgres:
    # PostgreSQL 15-18 supported; changing this major on an existing volume requires pg_upgrade
    image: postgres:15.8-alpine
    container_name: medikeep-db
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: ${DB_NAME:-medical_records}
      POSTGRES_USER: ${DB_USER:-medapp}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
      # For Docker secrets, use POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE instead (built-in to postgres image):
      #POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password
    volumes:
      - postgres_data-prod:/var/lib/postgresql/data
      - ./postgres/init.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init.sql:ro
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    healthcheck:
      test:
        [
          "CMD-SHELL",
          "pg_isready -U ${DB_USER:-medapp} -d ${DB_NAME:-medical_records}",
        ]
      interval: 60s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 30s
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks:
      - medikeep-network

  # Combined Frontend + Backend Application Service
  medikeep-app:
    image: ghcr.io/afairgiant/medikeep:latest
    # build:
    #   context: ..
    #   dockerfile: docker/Dockerfile
    container_name: medikeep-app
    ports:
      - ${APP_PORT:-8005}:8000 # Single port serves both React app and FastAPI
    environment:
      DB_HOST: postgres
      DB_PORT: 5432
      DB_NAME: ${DB_NAME:-medical_records}
      DB_USER: ${DB_USER:-medapp}
      DB_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
      SECRET_KEY: ${SECRET_KEY:?Set SECRET_KEY in .env or Docker secrets for persistent JWTs}
      DEBUG: ${DEBUG:-false}
      ENABLE_API_DOCS: ${ENABLE_API_DOCS:-false}
      LOG_LEVEL: ${LOG_LEVEL:-INFO}
      TZ: ${TZ:-America/New_York}
      # SSL Configuration - set ENABLE_SSL=true in .env to enable HTTPS
      ENABLE_SSL: ${ENABLE_SSL:-false}
      # Integration URL SSRF control - Paperless/Papra on private LAN addresses
      # is allowed by default; set false on internet-exposed instances to
      # restrict to public URLs (169.254.x cloud-metadata is always blocked).
      #ALLOW_PRIVATE_INTEGRATION_URLS: ${ALLOW_PRIVATE_INTEGRATION_URLS:-true}
      # SSO Configuration (Optional) - SSO is disabled by default
      SSO_ENABLED: ${SSO_ENABLED:-false}
      SSO_PROVIDER_TYPE: ${SSO_PROVIDER_TYPE:-oidc}
      SSO_CLIENT_ID: ${SSO_CLIENT_ID:-}
      SSO_CLIENT_SECRET: ${SSO_CLIENT_SECRET:-}
      SSO_ISSUER_URL: ${SSO_ISSUER_URL:-}
      SSO_REDIRECT_URI: ${SSO_REDIRECT_URI:-}
      SSO_ALLOWED_DOMAINS: ${SSO_ALLOWED_DOMAINS:-[]}

      # Default Admin Password Configuration (optional - defaults to admin123 in app if not set)
      #ADMIN_DEFAULT_PASSWORD: ${ADMIN_DEFAULT_PASSWORD:-}

      #PUID: ${PUID} # Enable if using bind mounts
      #PGID: ${PGID} # Enable if using bind mounts

      # --- Docker Secrets (_FILE pattern) ---
      # Instead of passing secrets as plain env vars, point to mounted files:
      #DB_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password
      #SECRET_KEY_FILE: /run/secrets/secret_key
      #SSO_CLIENT_ID_FILE: /run/secrets/sso_client_id
      #SSO_CLIENT_SECRET_FILE: /run/secrets/sso_client_secret
      #ADMIN_DEFAULT_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/admin_password
      # When using _FILE vars, remove the corresponding plain env var above.
    # secrets:
    #   - db_password
    #   - secret_key
    #   - sso_client_id
    #   - sso_client_secret
    #   - admin_password
    volumes:
      - app_uploads:/app/uploads
      - app_logs:/app/logs
      - app_backups:/app/backups

      # Uncomment the line below and create certificates if you want HTTPS
      # - ./certs:/app/certs:ro
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "-k", "http://localhost:8000/health"]
      interval: 120s
      timeout: 15s
      retries: 2
      start_period: 60s
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks:
      - medikeep-network

# Named volumes for data persistence
volumes:
  postgres_data-prod:
    driver: local
  app_uploads:
    driver: local
  app_logs:
    driver: local
  app_backups:
    driver: local

# --- Docker Secrets (uncomment to use with Docker Swarm or compose secrets) ---
# secrets:
#   db_password:
#     file: ./secrets/db_password.txt
#   secret_key:
#     file: ./secrets/secret_key.txt
#   sso_client_id:
#     file: ./secrets/sso_client_id.txt
#   sso_client_secret:
#     file: ./secrets/sso_client_secret.txt
#   admin_password:
#     file: ./secrets/admin_password.txt

# Network for service communication
networks:
  medikeep-network:
    driver: bridge
```

#### Create a .env file(or copy the env.example in the docker folder)

```bash
# Environment variables for Docker Compose
# Copy this file to .env and update the values

# Database Configuration
DB_NAME=medical_records
DB_USER=medapp
# IMPORTANT: Use quotes if password contains # (e.g., "my#pass")
# Always escape $ as $$ (e.g., pass$$word). Safe chars: @ % ^ & * ( ) - _ . !
DB_PASSWORD=your_secure_database_password_here #Change me

# Application port
APP_PORT=8005

# Application Security Key (REQUIRED - sessions are ephemeral without this)
SECRET_KEY=your-very-secure-secret-key-for-jwt-tokens-change-this-in-production

TZ=America/New_York
LOG_LEVEL=INFO #INFO or DEBUG
DEBUG=false
ENABLE_API_DOCS=false  # Set to true to expose Swagger docs
ENABLE_SSL=false # false or true
# Allow Paperless/Papra integrations on private LAN addresses (default true).
# Set false on internet-exposed/multi-user instances to restrict to public URLs.
# ALLOW_PRIVATE_INTEGRATION_URLS=true
```

### 3️⃣ Start the Containers

Run the following command to start the services:

```ini
docker compose up -d
```

Note: Do not use `docker-compose`.

### 4️⃣ Access the app

Once the containers are up, access the app in your browser at:

```ini
http://localhost:8005
```

### Default Login

On fresh installations, a default admin user is created:
- Username: `admin`
- Password: `admin123` (default)

**Customizing the Default Password:**

You can set a custom default admin password for fresh installations using the `ADMIN_DEFAULT_PASSWORD` environment variable:

```bash
# Set in your .env file or as environment variable
ADMIN_DEFAULT_PASSWORD=your_secure_password_here
```

**Note:** This only affects the initial admin user creation on fresh installations. It does not change passwords for existing users. Always change the default password after your first login.

## Backup and Restore

The app can be backed up using the Admin Dashboard.
Additionally, a backup/restore CLI is available.
This can be used with cron to automate scheduled backups.
See [Backup and Restore CLI](app/scripts/README_BACKUP_CLI.md) for more details.

Backups are stored under `/app/backups`. This should be mapped to
an external location or volume so that it can be stored safely in case a
restore is needed.

## SSO

The app has SSO capabilities.
As of right now, Google and Github are offically supported and tested.
ODIC SSO(keycloak, authlia, etc) should be supported but I haven't tested them yet.

See [SSO Quick Start](app/docs/SSO_QUICK_START.md) for google/github.

See [SSO Full Guide](app/docs/SSO_SETUP_GUIDE.md) for a more detailed guide.

repositories.readmeExcerpt:
# local-paas

An experimental, self-hosted application platform. Rust controller and node agents;
React, Vite, Tailwind and TanStack frontend. Licensed under [MIT](LICENSE).

Deploy Dockerfiles or supported Node, Bun, Python, Go, Rust, Ruby and PHP projects
from Git branches, tags, commits, or local uploads. Builds run in an isolated
BuildKit VM and produce immutable OCI images. Three isolated worker VMs run
applications through containerd. Management services run outside the cluster they
control.

## Install on Linux

The installation tooling targets **x86-64 and ARM64 Linux**, including Ubuntu,
Debian, Fedora and NixOS. It requires systemd, cgroup v2, KVM and the Nix package
manager. Nix provides pinned tools and VM images; the host does **not** need to run
NixOS. Installations currently use one architecture throughout the builder and
workers; mixed-architecture clusters and cross-building are not supported.

### Minimum host requirements

These requirements cover the default installation: one builder VM, three worker
VMs, and management services on the host.

| Resource | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| CPU | x86-64 or ARM64 with hardware virtualization accessible through `/dev/kvm`; VM hosts need nested virtualization |
| Memory | At least **16 GiB available RAM** before installation, after existing host services |
| Storage | At least **100 GiB free** on healthy local SSD/NVMe; check both the checkout and `/var/lib` filesystems |
| OS | Linux with systemd and cgroup v2, plus the Nix package manager |
| Access | An operator account with sudo and a working systemd user session; Internet access to download dependencies and images |

The builder uses 3 GiB RAM and 2 vCPUs; each worker uses 2 GiB RAM and 1 vCPU.
Each VM has a 16 GiB virtual disk. Allow additional memory and disk headroom for
compilation, application builds, databases, image caches, logs and retained
backups. These are installation requirements, not a workload capacity guarantee.
All four VMs initially share one physical host and failure domain.

Read **[the installation guide](docs/install.md)** first. It covers prerequisites,
private access, provisioning, reboot recovery, upgrades and removal.

From a fresh clone on a dedicated host/operator account:

```sh
nix develop
install -d -m 700 .local
cp platform.example.json .local/platform.json
# Edit .local/platform.json if using a private HTTPS dashboard/preview hostname.
make setup-check
make setup-install
```

`setup-check` is read-only. `setup-install` explicitly provisions the builder and
three workers, a dedicated PostgreSQL database, OpenBao, ClickHouse, registry,
node gateway and persistent systemd units. It uses sudo for VM isolation and host
units. It does not alter an existing Railway deployment, configure public DNS,
or enable off-site backups. Never run it to adopt an existing manually installed
stack; it refuses detected conflicts.

Open **http://localhost:5188**. For another machine, forward it over SSH or use
private HTTPS access as documented. The installed frontend serves built assets
through Caddy; it does not run the Vite development server.

This is a **private, multi-operator alpha**, not a public multi-tenant PaaS.
Operator sessions, organizations, and RBAC do not replace private network access. Keep management listeners on
loopback and restrict SSH/tailnet access to trusted operators. Three VMs on one
host are three scheduling nodes, not three physical failure domains.

## What works

- Projects, per-project environments, shadowed configuration and secrets.
- Dockerfile builds, versioned generated recipes for seven language ecosystems,
  build/start overrides and persisted detection evidence.
- Signed, replay-safe GitHub webhooks that pin repository events to commits.
- Opt-in same-repository PR previews with isolated multi-service templates, audited
  secret grants, GitHub Checks, quotas and durable cleanup.
- Health-gated deployments, retained revisions, failed-candidate rollback,
  independent ingress, cordon/drain and opt-in stateless relocation.
- Durable bounded crash/liveness recovery, replica health history and opt-in
  stateless replacement after restart-budget exhaustion.
- DNS-verified public OCI domains, Caddy API route updates, observed TLS and
  acknowledged promotion/rollback; explicit edge installation is required.
- Singleton workers, one-off jobs, interval schedules and pre-deployment commands.
- Opt-in CPU autoscaling and HTTP sleep/wake for eligible stateless services.
- OpenBao-backed workload secrets; dedicated ClickHouse runtime log retention.
- Structured log columns/search, retained instance logs, metrics and audit events.
- Managed PostgreSQL, Redis and RustFS; shared node-pinned volumes and file browsing.
- Encrypted local backups and restore drills for the documented subset of state.
- Remote Linux worker VMs over authenticated private links; see
  [remote setup and validation limits](docs/remote-workers.md).

Public VPS/NetBird installation remains explicit. The edge worker manages routes
on an operator-installed Caddy through its API. celld declarations are modeled separately, but fleet
execution is not implemented. Storage remains node-pinned. See
[architecture and release limits](docs/architecture.md), [runtime](docs/runtime.md),
[storage](docs/storage.md), [ingress](docs/ingress.md) and [backups](docs/backups.md).

See the [major PaaS feature comparison](docs/paas-comparison.md) for a sourced
comparison with managed and self-hosted platforms and links to tracked product
gaps.

## Develop without provisioning VMs

Use `nix develop` for the pinned Rust, Node, pnpm and PostgreSQL toolchain.
`mise install` pins language and package-manager versions when using native tools;
PostgreSQL 18 and Make/systemd are also needed.

```sh
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
make db
make bootstrap-auth
make api
make web
```

These targets supervise background development processes independently of the
terminal. The API binds `127.0.0.1:8080`; Vite binds `127.0.0.1:5188` and proxies the
API. Basic API/UI development works without OpenBao, ClickHouse or VMs; unavailable
infrastructure does not become fake successful builds or deployments.

The bootstrap reads passwords from ignored `.local/dev-auth.env` when present and
otherwise prompts without echoing them. For repeatable local credentials, install
`dev-auth.example.env` at that path with mode `0600` and edit its values; they may
be local-only passwords or 1Password CLI secret references. Authentication, organization,
team, custom-role, recovery, and threat-model details are in
[operator authentication](docs/authentication.md).

For foreground processes use `make api-foreground` / `make web-foreground`.
Checkout-specific operator configuration belongs in ignored `.local/platform.env`
(see [configuration](docs/install.md#configuration)). Application dotenv files are
never loaded by the controller. [Background services](docs/background-services.md)
explains installed and development service lifecycles.

## Validate

```sh
make check
# DATABASE_URL must point to a disposable PostgreSQL test database, with CREATEDB.
make test-db
```

`make check` runs Rust formatting, Clippy with warnings denied, workspace tests,
Oxfmt, Oxlint (including accessibility, React Doctor recommended and TanStack Query
rules), TypeScript, Vitest and the frontend
production build. Shared visual variants use CVA and `cn`; components are imported
directly, with no handwritten barrels. Oxlint also enforces one variable per statement.
Rule exceptions are documented beside the affected declaration or in
`web/oxlint.config.ts`; existing large views still need decomposition.
CI also runs nextest, doc tests, coverage, dependency/license
checks, secret scanning and generated OpenAPI/client drift checks.

For isolated browser tests, use a disposable PostgreSQL database named
`platform_test` or `platform_e2e`, with CREATEDB. The harness starts its own API,
OpenBao and web server; it does not use operator credentials or running workers.

```sh
cargo build -p control-plane --bins
nix build .#browser-test-tools --out-link /tmp/platform-browser-tools
pnpm --dir web exec playwright install --with-deps chromium firefox webkit
PATH="/tmp/platform-browser-tools/bin:$PATH" bash infra/tests/browser.sh
```

Infrastructure fault drills require explicit opt-in fixtures; they are not part
of ordinary local or CI tests. `pnpm --dir web test:coverage` reports unit coverage
without imposing an artificial universal threshold.

Compile-checked SQL uses reviewed metadata in `.sqlx`; normal builds run offline.
After changing a checked query or its schema, migrate a disposable test database,
then run `SQLX_OFFLINE=false cargo sqlx prepare --workspace -- --all-targets` with
`DATABASE_URL` pointing to it. CI checks the metadata against real PostgreSQL.

The API schema is exported to `docs/api/openapi.json`. Regenerate it and the Orval
TanStack Query client with `make api-schema` after changing documented endpoints.
This development release changes API fields to camelCase and agent protocol to v2;
existing installations require a [clean contract reset](docs/upgrades.md).

[Git provider automation](docs/git-automation.md) documents the current signed
GitHub webhook slice and its explicit private-repository limitations.

CI is configured for Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 on x86-64, and Ubuntu 24.04 on ARM64.
A fresh Ubuntu 24.04 x86-64 installation, real two-replica deployment and host
reboot recovery were verified. A native ARM64 installation/reboot drill is still
pending; CI configuration and Nix evaluation do not substitute for it. See
[validation status](docs/install.md#validation-status).

## Layout

| Directory | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `crates/domain`, `crates/protocol`, `crates/runtime` | Workload model and runtime-independent contracts |
| `crates/control-plane` | API, reconciliation, scheduling, ingress, operator commands |
| `crates/node-agent` | Privileged worker runtime, networking, health and telemetry |
| `crates/build-runner` | Isolated BuildKit execution and source detection |
| `infra` | Pinned tools, worker/builder images, service launchers and edge templates |
| `web` | React dashboard and shared controls |
| `docs`, `examples` | Operations, design constraints and canary fixtures |

# Local Code Tutor

### Fine-tune Qwen2.5-Coder-7B for free and run a coding agent that *runs your code instead of guessing* — on an 8 GB MacBook

[tests](https://github.com/pnnnx/local-code-tutor/actions)
python
model
training
runs on
license

**Execution-verified training data · QLoRA on a free GPU · GGUF on Apple Silicon · agent with measured fixes for 7B failure modes · LoRA/weight analysis with charts**

[Goal](#goal) · [At a glance](#at-a-glance) · [Results](#results) · [Quick start](#quick-start) · [How it works](#how-it-works) · [Lessons learned](#lessons-learned) · [Roadmap](#roadmap) · [Русская версия](README.ru.md)

## Meet Lo

   explains   mechanism,  why , the trap, the fix
   thinks out loud   you see the reasoning live
   grumpy mode   a tired senior, opt-in only
   looks inside   LoRA & weight charts
   olympiad mode   coming soon

Lo is the project mascot: a small terminal in a graduation cap — a tutor that lives on your laptop.

## Goal

**Give every student a private, free code tutor that runs on their own laptop — and never states
something about code that it hasn't checked.**

A 2nd-year student shouldn't need a paid cloud subscription to get a patient explanation of *why*
their code behaves the way it does. This project aims to show that a **7B model on an 8 GB laptop**
can be that tutor — if the system around it is built so the model doesn't have to guess:

- **Explain, don't paraphrase** — name the language mechanism, show *why* step by step, point out the
  trap, give the fix. In the student's own language.
- **Verify, don't guess** — outputs, errors and "is it done?" come from running code, never from the
  model's memory.
- **Go beyond toy snippets** — whole programs ("how does this system work?"), data analysis
  (pandas, SQL, dashboards) and looking *inside* neural networks with charts.
- **Reproducible for $0** — a recipe anyone can repeat: free GPU for training, local inference, every
  decision and measurement documented.

  Text version

**Definition of done for `v1.0`** — each item is measurable with the tools in this repo:

| Goal | Target | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Key facts on held-out questions | ≥ 15 / 18 | 13 / 18 |
| Agent asks instead of guessing on vague requests | 4 / 4 | ✅ 4 / 4 |
| "What will this print?" answered from a real run | 100 % | ✅ 2 / 2 |
| Multi-file tasks finished by the plan, not by luck | 4 / 4 hard tasks | measuring |
| Verified examples, incl. Java, SQL analytics, PyTorch | ≥ 2,000 | 1,581 |
| Runs fully offline on a MacBook Air M2 8 GB | yes | yes |

**Non-goals:** competing with frontier cloud models on large refactors or deep reasoning; being a
general-purpose chatbot. The target is narrow on purpose — *understanding code you're learning from*.

## At a glance

  Text version

**Release `v0.3.0`**

| Component | Version | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **local-code-tutor** (this repo) | `0.3.0` | beta |
| **[loca](https://github.com/pnnnx/loca)** agent | `0.1.0` · 106 tests | beta |
| **wtools** weight analysis | `0.1.0` · 5 commands · MCP | beta |
| Fine-tuned model **my-coder** | `v3` · LoRA r=32 · 954 + 300 examples | experimental |
| Dataset format | `v1` · 7 kinds · 6 languages | stable |
| Held-out eval | `v1` · 18 questions · auto-scored | stable |

**Tested with**

| Stack | Version |
|---|---|
| Base model | Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct |
| Training | Unsloth QLoRA 4-bit · Kaggle T4 16 GB · fp16 |
| Inference | llama.cpp `0.7.0-dev` (`1b29621`) · Ollama |
| Quantization | GGUF `Q4_K_M` · 4.4 GB file · ~4.7 GB RAM |
| Python | `3.9` – `3.13` (loca: stdlib only) |
| PyTorch | `2.14` CPU · safetensors `0.8` · matplotlib `3.11` |
| Hardware | MacBook Air M2 **8 GB** · Kaggle T4 |

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Verified training examples | **1,581** and growing (target ≈ 2,600) across 20+ categories |
| Held-out key facts, base → v2 → v3 | **8 / 18 → 9 / 15 → 13 / 18** ([details](docs/RESULTS.md)) |
| Agent failure mode #8 "guesses instead of asking" | **1 / 4 → 4 / 4** on real Qwen2.5-Coder-7B |
| Agent failure mode #4 "can't run code in its head" | **0 / 1 → 2 / 2** on real Qwen2.5-Coder-7B |
| Cost | **$0** — free Kaggle GPU, local inference |

---

Small local models are great at *sounding* right. Ask a 7B model "what does this print?" and it will
confidently invent the output. This project is built around one rule:

  Text version

> **The model never guesses what code does. Something always runs it.**

| Where | How the rule is enforced |
|---|---|
| **Training data** | Every example is executed (Python, JS, C/C++, Java, SQLite). If the answer disagrees with the real output, the example is dropped. Near-duplicates are caught by comparing code *skeletons* (identifiers → `ID`, literals → `S`/`N`). |
| **Agent** | When you ask "what will this print / why does it crash", the [loca](https://github.com/pnnnx/loca) agent shows the model the source **and runs it before the model answers**. Unsafe code (deletes files, network, `input()`) is never auto-run. |
| **Evaluation** | 18 held-out questions that never appear in training, scored automatically on key facts. |

Everything below runs on a **MacBook Air M2 with 8 GB RAM**; training uses the **free Kaggle T4**.

  Diagram source (Mermaid)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[LLM writes candidate examples] --> B[run every snippet compare real output skeleton dedup]
  B --> C[verified dataset]
  C --> D[QLoRA on free Kaggle T4 · Unsloth]
  D --> E[GGUF Q4_K_M 4.4 GB]
  E --> F[llama.cpp / Ollama 8 GB Mac]
  F --> G[loca agent]
  H[weights tools stats · diff · LoRA · quant] -- MCP --> G
```

## Results

All numbers are measured, including the ones that didn't go my way.

### 1. Fixing 7B failure modes inside the agent

Measured on the real thing: **Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct Q4_K_M** in `llama-server`, with a probe
harness that runs the same requests before and after each fix (`bench/probe.py` in loca).

- **#8 "Guesses instead of asking" — 1/4 → 4/4.** On vague requests ("add promo codes") the model
  invented a goal and even marked existing files as "(new)". Fix: a *task spec* step (goal, files,
  constraints, a runnable done-check, assumptions, questions) plus deterministic post-checks that don't
  trust the model — paths are verified against the disk, and a vague request with no questions gets one.
  Now the model itself asks: *which promo codes, where are they stored, how do they affect the total?*
- **#4 "Can't execute code in its head" — 0/1 → 2/2.** A "run it first" reminder was simply **ignored**:
  asked about `tricky.py`, the model replied *"that file doesn't exist"* without calling a single tool.
  Fix: the agent runs the code itself and puts the source + real output in context before the model speaks.

### 2. Fine-tuning: v2 learned the *form*, v3 got the *facts*, v4 hit a plateau

**v2** answered exactly in the target style (verdict first, precise mechanism, fixed code) — **but
confidently invented outputs**: `[3, 3, 3]` instead of `[2, 2, 2]`, "6" instead of 14. **v3** added
pandas, SQLite analytics, PyTorch and weight-analysis examples: late binding is now right, the SQL
answer uses SQLite's `STRFTIME` + `LAG`, the PyTorch questions pass. It **still can't do arithmetic in
its head** (e07, e13) — which is exactly why the agent runs code instead of trusting the model.

**v4** (1,581 examples, +66 %: pandas, dashboards, SQL analytics, systems, Java) scored **the same 13/18 on exactly
the same questions**. Every remaining miss is a *concrete value invented in the head* — a sum, a printed loss,
which rows a query returns. More explanation data doesn't fix that; running the code does. The held-out set is
also too Python-basics-heavy to see what v4 added, so the next eval version gets Java, pandas and dashboard questions.
Details: [docs/RESULTS.md](docs/RESULTS.md).

### 3. Look inside the network — with charts

`wtools/weights.py` (CLI + MCP server, so the agent can call it):

  Text version

| Command | What you learn |
|---|---|
| `inspect` | tensors, shapes, dtypes, memory at fp32 / fp16 / int8 / int4, biggest blocks |
| `stats` | per-layer scale, >6σ outliers, dead neurons, sparsity, weight histogram |
| `diff` | what fine-tuning changed: ‖ΔW‖/‖W‖ and cosine per layer and per module type |
| `lora` | ΔW = B·A·α/r per module, effective rank, energy in the top direction, spectrum — via QR on r×r, fast even for 7B |
| `quant` | int8/int4 error per layer: per-tensor vs per-row vs 32-block scales (the GGUF idea) |

 Real output of `wtools` on a 12-layer toy model (`scripts/brand/wtools_demo.py`). The agent can't see images, so every number on a chart is also
printed as text — the model explains the chart from the numbers.

## Quick start

**Analyze a LoRA adapter or a checkpoint** (any PEFT adapter / safetensors / `.pt`):

```bash
pip install torch safetensors matplotlib
python3 wtools/weights.py lora   path/to/lora_adapter        # what did fine-tuning actually do?
python3 wtools/weights.py diff   base.safetensors tuned.safetensors
python3 wtools/weights.py quant  model.safetensors --bits 4
```

**Fine-tune your own tutor on a free GPU:** open `kaggle_qwen_coder_finetune_v2.ipynb` on Kaggle
(GPU T4 × 1), upload your `explain_*.jsonl`, *Run All*. You get a LoRA adapter, a held-out evaluation
and a `Q4_K_M` GGUF ready for llama.cpp / Ollama.

**Build a verified dataset:**

```bash
cd ds && ./ds.sh            # pick a topic → prompt goes to clipboard → paste the LLM's answer back
./ds.sh status              # coverage per category vs targets
./ds.sh build               # re-run everything, dedup, write the training file
```

**Run it locally with the agent:**

```bash
llama-server -m my-coder-v2-Q4_K_M.gguf --jinja -c 8192 -fa on -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0
loca --backend llamacpp                     # https://github.com/pnnnx/loca
python3 wtools/install_loca.py              # give the agent the weight-analysis tools
```

## How it works

  Text version

1. A prompt with the category, topics, *what is already covered* and strict format rules goes to an
   LLM (ChatGPT or Claude) via the clipboard.
2. The answer is parsed and **every snippet is executed** in a sandboxed temp dir (`runner.py`).
3. `build.py` rejects an example if: the stated output doesn't match the real one, it crashes without
   naming the exception, the "write code" answer doesn't contain the code, it's a skeleton-duplicate of
   anything already accepted, it's too close to a held-out question, or it's too short / long / watery.
4. Rejections are turned into a "fix these" message for the same chat; accepted examples are committed
   to git automatically with the rejection reasons in the commit message.

**Training (`kaggle_qwen_coder_finetune_v2.ipynb`)** — Unsloth QLoRA on `Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct`,
fp16 on T4, `adamw_8bit`, loss on responses only, half of the examples with a system prompt so the model
behaves the same with and without it; then automatic held-out eval and GGUF export.

**The agent ([loca](https://github.com/pnnnx/loca))** — a stdlib-only terminal coding agent
for small local models: repo map with signatures and tests per file, read-by-symbol, fuzzy edits, a
plan graph with executable acceptance checks and rollbacks, sub-agents, undo snapshots, hooks, MCP,
Ollama and llama.cpp backends. 106 tests.

## Lessons learned

  Text version

- **A 7B model ignores polite reminders.** "Run the code first" in the prompt changed nothing; doing it
  deterministically in the harness fixed it. Prefer code paths over prompt paths for anything critical.
- **Fine-tuning teaches style long before facts.** 762 examples were enough to change *how* the model
  answers, not enough to make it right more often. Put the verdict *after* a short trace, not before.
- **Verify with execution, not with another LLM.** A judge model says "looks correct"; a Python
  process prints the truth.
- **Measure on the real model.** Every fix that "obviously worked" in unit tests failed at least once on
  the actual 7B before
